rationale: This qualitative socio-historical case study (1990-2022) examines drinking water management in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri, Costa Rica, drawing on institutional files, water quality laboratory reports, qualitative interviews, and community workshops. Multiple rule and governance mechanisms are co-equally analyzed to explain service failures: community water committee governance, user participation, Indigenous consultation rules, and state technical/intercultural accompaniment (participation_assistance, primary), Costa Rica's delegated community aqueduct/ASADA model and lack of Indigenous legal personality (regulatory_model_ownership), centralized and intermittent multi-agency state interventions by AyA and the Ministry of Health misaligned with Indigenous territorial governance (institutional_structure_coordination), unsubsidized flat-tariff cost-recovery rules and disputes over tariff levels and metering (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and sanitary orders/inspections (enforcement_sanctions). The central empirical outcome analyzed throughout is effective access—specifically persistent non-potability (fecal coliform contamination), seasonal water availability, and functional sustainability of the aqueduct system.
